action->Jaunty Jig.name: Jaunty Jig
action->Jaunty Jig.description:
The kirakor dances, rubbing its legs together to emit a pleasant tune that inspires listeners to join in. Each non-fey creature within a @Template[type:emanation|distance:30] must attempt a @Check[will|dc:17] save. A kirakor can Sustain this effect for up to 1 minute, and the first time each round that the kirakor Sustains the effect in subsequent rounds, each non-fey creature in the emanation must attempt the save again.

Critical Success The creature is unaffected and is temporarily immune for 1 minute.

Success The creature is unaffected.

Failure The creature dances, becoming @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.AJh5ex99aV6VTggg]{Off-Guard} and taking a –10-foot circumstance penalty to all its Speeds for 1 round.

Critical Failure As failure, and the creature becomes @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.xYTAsEpcJE1Ccni3]{Slowed 1}.

Kishi.name: Kishi
Kishi.publicNotes:
Kishis are duplicitous, murderous fey who dwell on the edges of Golarion's densest jungles. At first glance, kishis appear to be attractive humans, usually of a local ethnicity, but their full heads of thick hair conceal a second face: that of a snarling hyena. When a kishi lures their prey into a vulnerable situation, their head swivels around, revealing this fearsome visage. In this form, a kishi's powerful jaws are almost impossible to pry loose and can crush a victim's bones in a matter of moments.

Kishis range widely in their physical features, and their height and weight vary as much as the people whose communities they infiltrate. They dress in fine clothing aligned with the latest fashion trends, and they wear flashy jewelry to draw onlookers' eyes.

Like most fey, kishis have inscrutable motives, though to their victims, their goal seems simple—to revel in the expression of shock, betrayal, and terror on a victim's face. Although kishis can cast @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.spells-srd.Item.vLA0q0WOK2YPuJs6]{Charm} to make unwitting companions complacent, most of these sinister creatures prefer to trick their prey using guile, gifts, and their dashing good looks. These ultimate sadists derive pleasure from the thrill of the hunt as much as the delicious reward at the end. The more uptight, prudish, or haughty a target, the better—for nothing satisfies kishis as much as earning (and destroying) the trust of someone who rarely grants it.

When kishis get their new friends or lovers alone, they choose the most dramatic moments to reveal their true monstrous forms and clamp their jaws down on their victim. Kishis have no desire to share their true nature with the entire community, so they typically aim for the throat to keep their victim from crying out for help. The fey then consume every part of their victims' bodies, leaving no trace of the crime—even lapping up any spilled blood, claiming the victim's treasures as their own, and cleaning the murder scene as much as possible.

Few things can bind a community together as swiftly as uncovering a kishi. Once found out, a kishi flees, hoping to find a new community to prey upon.

spell->Charm (At Will).name:

action->Head Spin.name: Head Spin
action->Head Spin.description: The kishi switches between showing their attractive human face and their snarling hyena face. A kishi can use their innate spell and their Deception and Diplomacy skills only when their human face is showing, and they can use their jaws Strike only when their hyena face is showing.

action->Sudden Charge.name: Sudden Charge
action->Sudden Charge.description: The kishi Strides twice. If they end their movement within melee reach of at least one enemy, they can make a melee Strike against that enemy.

action->Vicelike Jaws.name: Vicelike Jaws
action->Vicelike Jaws.description: A creature @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.kWc1fhmv9LBiTuei]{Grabbed} in the kishi's jaws can barely speak; a creature must succeed at a @Check[flat|dc:8] to speak or cast spells, doing so in a choked whisper.

Laluxi.name: Laluxi
Laluxi.languages: Telepathy 100 feet (doesnt need to share a language)
Laluxi.publicNotes:
Laluxis, also whispered of as "dream scribes" by those few who survive an encounter with one, are ancient, almost-mythical beings who dwell in the drifting silk islands of the Astral Tangle—the volatile borderlands where the First World and the Astral Plane mix.

Laluxis are prophets, poets, and wielders of thought, collecting the dreams and nightmares of fey and mortals alike on their long journeys. They don't speak so much as write into the minds of their victims, filling their heads with lifetimes of dreams through a mere glance. Where they go, dream and reality unravel into thread and tangle together, and minds stretched too tightly might snap.

Laluxis are beautiful creatures of fine fur and featureless black carapaces, with elegant humanoid arms and four shimmering, colorful wings. Their awe-inspiring presence means they're sometimes mistaken for divine messengers. In truth, they serve only their own cryptic purposes, gathering the finest subconscious castoffs to weave into their ever-growing cosmological tapestry.

spell->Dreaming Potential (At Will).name:
<Compendium> tag will get replaced with text from compendium entry @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.spells-srd.Item.y0Vy7iNL3ET8K00C]

spell->Illusory Scene (At WIll).name:
<Compendium> tag will get replaced with text from compendium entry @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.spells-srd.Item.Ucf8eynbZMfUucjE]

action->Astral Stitch.name: Astral Stitch
action->Astral Stitch.description: 30 feet. A laluxi's presence subtly alters the world around them, weaving the stuff of dreams into reality. Illusions within the emanation are distorted and become slightly more real, imposing a –2 circumstance penalty to saves against them and to saves or checks to disbelieve them.

action->Flickerwing.name: Flickerwing
action->Flickerwing.description:
Trigger The laluxi is targeted by an attack

Effect The laluxi disappears in a whirl of light and threads, gaining a +2 circumstance bonus to AC against the triggering attack. If the attack misses, the laluxi can teleport up to 20 feet; this is a teleportation effect.

action->Starweaver's Lure.name: Starweaver's Lure
action->Starweaver's Lure.description:
Frequency once per round

Effect The laluxi conjures a cascade of refracted dreams and starlight threads, hurling it at a creature within 60 feet. The target must succeed at a @Check[will|dc:36] save or be @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.AdPVz7rbaVSRxHFg]{Fascinated} by the laluxi for 1 minute. While fascinated, the target can't end any move action farther from the laluxi than where it started.

action->Steal Dreams.name: Steal Dreams
action->Steal Dreams.description:
Frequency once per hour

Effect The laluxi snaps their great wings open, siphoning threads of dreams and nightmares from creatures that witness them. Each creature in a @Template[type:cone|distance:30] takes @Damage[12d6[mental]|options:area-damage] damage with a @Check[will|dc:36|basic] save. A creature that fails the save is also @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.e1XGnhKNSQIm5IXg]{Stupefied 2} for 1 minute.

Lurker In Light.name: Lurker In Light
Lurker In Light.publicNotes:
As easily as a Darklands predator hides in the unsettling mystery of shadows, a lurker in light disappears into the brightest light. These malicious and strange fey appear as fairies about 2 feet tall, with insectile wings, large eyes, and bulbous heads. They slaughter and cause mischief in patterns only their alien intellect understands, but they've been seen to take particular umbrage with dwarves, gnomes, and creatures who live in darkness. With their relentless grudges and pursuit of their own wicked and sadistic whims, lurkers in light deftly overturn the conventional wisdom that creatures associated with light are benign and friendly.

Though lurkers in light are fey and have ties to the First World, these creatures are often found elsewhere in the Great Beyond. They're particularly fond of invading the Netherworld to bring light to those who dwell there—not to help, but to spread misery and pain among those to whom light is agonizing.

spell->Translocate (Only when in bright.name:
<Compendium> tag will get replaced with text from compendium entry @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.spells-srd.Item.VlNcjmYyu95vOUe8]
Translocate (Only when in bright light, and only to an area in bright light)

action->Blend with Light.name: Blend with Light
action->Blend with Light.description:
Trigger The lurker in light uses a move action

Requirements The lurker in light is in an area of bright light

Effect The lurker in light becomes invisible until they enter an area of dim light or darkness, or until they use a hostile action.

action->Lurker's Glow.name: Lurker's Glow
action->Lurker's Glow.description:
A creature that takes damage from a lurker in light's mote of light Strike must attempt a @Check[will|dc:22] save.

Success The creature is unaffected and is temporarily immune to lurker's glow for 24 hours.

Failure The creature is lined in golden light for 1 minute and can't be @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.DmAIPqOBomZ7H95W]{Concealed} during this time. If the creature becomes invisible, it's concealed rather than undetected.

Critical Failure As failure, but the creature sheds bright light in a @Template[type:emanation|distance:20] for the duration of the effect. In addition, the creature is @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.TkIyaNPgTZFBCCuh]{Dazzled} until the end of its next turn.

action->Ritual Gate.name: Ritual Gate
action->Ritual Gate.description:
Requirements The lurker in light has reduced a living creature to 0 Hit Points on this turn or their previous turn and has a @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.spells-srd.Item.hs7h8f4Z1ZNdUt3s]{Summon Fey} innate spell available

Effect The lurker in light casts summon fey with only a concentrate trait, using the act of slaughter to replace the normal manipulate traits for the spell. If the fey creature summoned shares the lurker in light's current goals, the lurker in light can sustain the summon fey spell for up to 1 hour instead of 1 minute.

action->Sneak Attack.name: Sneak Attack
action->Sneak Attack.description: A lurker in light's Strikes deal an additional 2d6 precision damage to @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.AJh5ex99aV6VTggg]{Off-Guard} creatures.

Mari Lwyd.name: Mari Lwyd
Mari Lwyd.publicNotes: Winter celebrants beware! A song at the door may herald the arrival of a mari lwyd, a shrouded creature with a grinning, horse-like skull. Despite their macabre visage, these fey singers mean no harm, wishing only to join in with seasonal festivities and partake in hospitality. They're especially partial to alcohol and cheese but can be appeased with other treats if the household has none.

action->Gracious Guest.name: Gracious Guest
action->Gracious Guest.description: The mari lwyd will not pass through a closed threshold without first receiving permission to do so, though they can compel permission using Pwnco.

action->Mostly Harmless.name: Mostly Harmless
action->Mostly Harmless.description: The mari lwyd is out to enjoy the season but becomes dangerous if provoked. Their attacks lose the nonlethal trait against creatures that have damaged them and objects.

action->Persistent Wassailing.name: Persistent Wassailing
action->Persistent Wassailing.description: The mari lwyd is immune to any effect that would prevent them from singing or prevent others from hearing their song.

action->Festive Rampage.name: Festive Rampage
action->Festive Rampage.description:
Requirements The mari lwyd gained permission to enter a structure

Effect The mari lwyd Strides or Swims to enter the structure and goes on a celebratory rampage, smashing furniture and dishware. They then gain resistance 10 to all damage (except cold iron), and their attacks ignore 10 Hardness of any objects they encounter. The effect lasts until the mari lwyd leaves the structure, damages a living creature, or is offered food and drink.

action->Joyous Procession.name: Joyous Procession
action->Joyous Procession.description: The mari lwyd Strides, compelling nearby creatures to join their celebration. Each creature in a @Template[type:emanation|distance:10] at the start of the Stride must succeed at a @Check[will|dc:30] save or use its first action on its next turn to Stride directly toward the mari lwyd.

action->Pwnco.name: Pwnco
action->Pwnco.description:
The mari lwyd begins a rhyming contest, requesting entrance to a structure from creatures within. Before the start of the mari lwyd's next turn, at least one occupant can spend 2 actions to [[/act perform dc=33]] a song of their own; the DC is equal to the mari lwyd's Performance DC. If multiple occupants attempt the check, the group takes the highest result. If no occupant spends actions to respond, the group critically fails. Determine the results at the start of the mari lwyd's turn.

Critical Success The respondents win the Pwnco, and the mari lwyd can't enter the structure for 1 month.

Success The response is good, and the Pwnco continues. The mari lwyd must use Pwnco again on their next turn, taking a circumstance penalty to their Performance DC equal to double the number of times they have used Pwnco to attempt to enter the structure today.

Failure The respondents lose. The door unlocks and opens, and any nonmagical barriers move out of the way. If the door is magically sealed, the mari lwyd attempts to counteract the effect (counteract rank 6, counteract modifier [[/r 1d20+22 #Counteract]]{+22}).

Critical Failure As failure, but the mari lwyd gets a result one degree of success better than they roll for any attempts to counteract magical barriers.

Marraine.name: Marraine
Marraine.publicNotes:
The stories are as common as they are unlikely: the mysterious noble who won the heart of a prince at a courtly ball is revealed to be the humble third son of a miller and rises to a station beyond his wildest dreams. A proud elf turns an elderly visitor away and is cursed to transform into a hideous beast, cured only when she finds "true love," and with it, happiness her wealth could never bring.

In truth, most of these stories are the machinations of fey marraines. These courtiers of the First World make up the councils marraine, a loose confederation of fey nobility who compete in a complicated game of status that mostly hinges on the bragging rights secured by ensuring the happiness and prosperity of their chosen "pet" mortals, which they call their godchildren.

While nominally benevolent, relations can quickly sour if a marraine's mortal charge disagrees with their self-proclaimed godparent's designs. Those who accept a marraine's initial gifts but reject their future meddling, or who seek to escape a "happily ever after" they've come to regret, quickly find their former benefactor enacting vengeance through powerful magic or fey allies.

weapon->Marraine Wand.description: A light mace has a short wooden or metal shaft ending with a dense metal head. Used much like a club, it delivers heavy bludgeoning blows, but with extra power derived from the head's metal ridges or spikes.

action->Council Marraine.name: Council Marraine
action->Council Marraine.description: For their mutual benefit, marraines form councils of exactly three or seven members. A council marraine acts as a hag's coven but has the arcane trait instead of occult and their granted spells also include @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.spells-srd.Item.TUj8eugNqAvB1vVR]{Creation}, @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.spells-srd.Item.Ucf8eynbZMfUucjE]{Illusory Scene}, and @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.spells-srd.Item.r784cIz17eWujtQj]{Scrying}. If the council has seven members, @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.spells-srd.Item.5c692cCcTDXjSEzk]{dragon form,} @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.spells-srd.Item.HES5jvGiNZZnJycK]{Lifewood Cage}, and @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.spells-srd.Item.vPWMEyVTreMOoFnm]{Planar Palace} are also added to their granted spells, and when council members Cast @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.spells-srd.Item.dN8QBNuTiaBHCKUe]{Cursed Metamorphosis} as a coven spell, they can transform targets into sentient animated objects as well as harmless animals, and can transform animals or objects into humanoids. If a creature critically fails, their transformation into an object ends at the next midnight or sunrise (depending on the council's bylaws).

action->Sudden Appearance.name: Sudden Appearance
action->Sudden Appearance.description:
Frequency once per week

Requirements The target is in the Universe, and the marraine is in either the First World or the Universe

Effect The marraine teleports to an unoccupied space within 30 feet of a creature they've marked as their godchild. They must have previously seen the target, typically with a @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.spells-srd.Item.zvKWclOZ7A53DObE]{Clairvoyance} or @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.spells-srd.Item.r784cIz17eWujtQj]{Scrying} spell.

Melixie.name: Melixie
Melixie.publicNotes:
Melixies are hyperactive insect sprites with legendary sweet tooths, capable of gulping down honey, nectar, sugar, and other sweets in alarming quantities. Melixies have antennae and additional insect features that typically resemble those of bees but sometimes butterflies, moths, ladybugs, or other beetles. Melixies live in a pattern of rapid sweets consumption, incredible productivity in tasks of all sorts, and then a crash to sleep it all off and start again. In their spare time, they love to dance, and some learn a dancelike sign language called Melipatter, allowing them to communicate a full range of information through movement.

Elusive, flighty, and ebullient, sprites are what many villagers first imagine when they hear the terms "fey" or "fairy."

action->Speak with Arthropods.name: Speak with Arthropods
action->Speak with Arthropods.description: A melixie can communicate with arthropods, such as insects, spiders, scorpions, crabs, and similar invertebrate animals. They can use Diplomacy to [[/act make-an-impression]] on arthropods and [[/act request]] things from arthropods.

action->Sugar Rush.name: Sugar Rush
action->Sugar Rush.description: The melixie consumes a large quantity of sugar, honey, nectar, or similar sweets and goes into a frenzied state. The melixie immediately Strides or Flies. For the next [[/gmr 1d4+1 #rounds]] rounds, the melixie is @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.nlCjDvLMf2EkV2dl]{Quickened} and can use the additional action only to Stride or Fly. As soon as the rush ends, the melixie is @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.HL2l2VRSaQHu9lUw]{Fatigued} for 1 minute.

Monaciello.name: Monaciello
Monaciello.publicNotes:
Monaciellos delight in moral and institutional decay. They tempt with the easy course, encouraging laziness and apathy. They're the little voice that whispers that no one will notice, that it's not really worth the effort, that there's a quicker, easier solution if you just try just a little less hard.

Monaciellos resemble small, sharp-toothed humanoids clad in the formal clothing of whatever institution or organization they're harassing. Most dress like religious figures—there's nothing a monaciello loves quite so much as a church lost to decadence and self-indulgence—but a monaciello might also pose as a well-to-do farmer, a civil servant, or even a soldier. There's always something slovenly and unkempt about their uniform of choice, and they keep a filthy magic bag thrown over one shoulder or near at hand. Monaciellos cause endless trouble by stealing small items, secreting them in their sack, and then bringing them out at the perfect moment to tempt mortals into indolence and sloth. These items are rarely impressive, but the gremlins always seem to have a drink or gold coin at hand when a mortal craves it most.

Like many fey, gremlins personify a natural force of the world: entropy. It's a fundamental truth that everything breaks, that every complex system, from a machine to a society, will inevitably grind itself down to nothing. Gremlins are happy to give those complex systems a friendly shove down the stairs.

Nearly all gremlins live in the Universe, where they have fully acclimated to the plane. No one is quite certain why, but it seems likely that some long-forgotten gremlin managed to so irritate the Eldest to such a degree that their entire species was exiled—though it appears the Eldest missed a few, as some gremlins still lurk in the First World.

Gremlins are usually found in an odd, parasitic relationship with mortal communities in the Universe. They don't need to eat or sleep, don't age or sicken, and never really die—but they do need to cause trouble. It's as essential to them as food and drink are to mortals, and nowhere do they get as many chances for chaos and confusion as in a mortal settlement. Gremlins thus become pests, living on the margins of society and bedeviling anyone and anything they can get their hands on.
Monaciello.saveDetails: +1 status to all saves vs. divine magic

action->Magic Sack.name: Magic Sack
action->Magic Sack.description: A monaciello's sack functions as a @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.equipment-srd.Item.jaEEvuQ32GjAa8jy]{Spacious Pouch (Type I)} as long as it's in the monaciello's possession. If the sack is separated from the monaciello, its contents are lost and it becomes a normal bag. A monaciello who loses their bag must create a new one, a process that takes 2 days.

action->+1 Status to All Saves vs. Divin.name: +1 Status to All Saves vs. Divine Magic

action->Rude Blasphemy.name: Rude Blasphemy
action->Rude Blasphemy.description:
Trigger A creature within 30 feet casts a divine spell

Effect The monaciello makes a blasphemous gesture tailor-made to offend the target's religion, attempting to counteract the spell (counteract modifier [[/r 1d20+6 #Counteract]]{+6}, counteract rank 1st). The monaciello can't use Rude Blasphemy again for [[/gmr 1d4 #Recharge Rude Blasphemy]]{1d4 rounds}.

action->Heart's Desire.name: Heart's Desire
action->Heart's Desire.description:
Frequency once per day

Effect The monaciello pulls a desirable object from its sack. Each creature within 15 feet who can see the object immediately covets it and must attempt a @Check[will|dc:17] save. If the monaciello spends two actions on Heart's Desire, this must be a real object already in their possession. If they spend three actions, they can cast illusory object as part of the activity, which gains the subtle trait.

Critical Success The target is unaffected.

Success The target is @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.xYTAsEpcJE1Ccni3]{Slowed 1} for 1 round.

Failure The target is slowed 1 for 1 round and, if it doesn't have a free hand, must spend its first action on its next turn to Release one item it's holding to grab for the object instead.

Critical Failure As failure, but the target is @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.xYTAsEpcJE1Ccni3]{Slowed 2} instead.

Murxie.name: Murxie
Murxie.publicNotes:
Sprite

The fey of the Ether Court in the Darklands have evolved somewhat differently from the First World kin that exiled them, becoming more cruel and less mischievous than is typical for their kind.

Ether Sprite

The excitable sprites of the Ether Court prefer to frolic, drink, insult each other, and perform improv comedy.

Sprite Collections

Ether sprites have a reputation for being thieves. In truth, they're generally curious about the world and simply have a tendency to walk away with objects that don't belong to them, not understanding the concept of ownership. As a result, ether sprites tend to have small interesting objects in their possession, such as talismans or gemstones.

action->Natural Glow.name: Natural Glow

Nornhounds are massive wolves norns spun from the old, tattered threads of fate, usually moments of time severed to end a life. These wolves gain a portion of their creators' power over fate and serve their norn masters with unflinching loyalty.

Where their masters snip and mend threads of fate with subtlety and precision, nornhounds do so brutally and forcefully, overwhelming their foes with blasts and waves of skipped time and overlapping possibilities. A mortal who faces down a nornhound often finds themselves with permanent mental effects, remembering lives that aren't their own or responding to questions a second before they're asked.

Nornhound Packs

Long-lived or powerful norns sometimes spin multiple nornhounds and keep entire packs as guardians. These packs make quick work of intruders, gaining additional powers when working together. Much like a norn triumvirate, a nornhound pack can combine their power to affect the flow of time in a localized area, even stopping it outright. These packs are rarely found far from the domains of their masters, but those who survive an encounter find the experience impossible to describe to others.

The "towering" hunchbacked nuglubs are among the largest gremlins, though they're not even 3 feet tall. They have three glowing blue eyes and black, oily hair on their head and back that covers them like a cloak. Nuglubs enjoy killing with a glee that other gremlins reserve for sabotage. They spend long hours preparing ambushes for unwary travelers or plotting the murders of sleeping villagers. Though less technically inclined than their kin, nuglubs do enjoy building traps.

Like many fey, gremlins personify a natural force of the world: entropy. It's a fundamental truth that everything breaks, that every complex system, from a machine to a society, will inevitably grind itself down to nothing. Gremlins are happy to give those complex systems a friendly shove down the stairs.

Nearly all gremlins live in the Universe, where they have fully acclimated to the plane. No one is quite certain why, but it seems likely that some long-forgotten gremlin managed to so irritate the Eldest to such a degree that their entire species was exiled—though it appears the Eldest missed a few, as some gremlins still lurk in the First World.

Gremlins are usually found in an odd, parasitic relationship with mortal communities in the Universe. They don't need to eat or sleep, don't age or sicken, and never really die—but they do need to cause trouble. It's as essential to them as food and drink are to mortals, and nowhere do they get as many chances for chaos and confusion as in a mortal settlement. Gremlins thus become pests, living on the margins of society and bedeviling anyone and anything they can get their hands on.

Violating a nyktera's hospitality is one of their greatest taboos, inviting rare anger and retribution from the nyktera who was wronged, as well as their large extended family.

They ride the open waves as naturally as dolphins and live among the deepest depths without care for cold, darkness, or pressure. As such, they're a rare and mysterious sight for those mortals who dwell on land but well-known to denizens of the sea, such as merfolk, for whom they're often confused.

Oceanids can be as tempestuous as their watery home, with moods that change on a whim. They're quick to love and even quicker to anger. At heart, however, they're nurturing guardians, especially to the young, the elderly, the injured, and the desperate. It's not unheard of for oceanids to take in and raise children who've been abandoned near the shore, and sailors who speak of them with respect often miraculously survive storms and sinkings that otherwise leave no survivors.

The riotous clamor of stone against stone in the First World often heralds the presence of a hidden pech quarry. While peches may use tools and their innate magic for mining and construction, such is the extent of their practicality. These subterranean fey are otherwise wholly committed to using their bodies alone to refine earthen bounty, crushing stone bare-handed and cutting gemstones against their muscles to create art. To chisel and polish their muscles of stone, peches pursue their crafts with near obsession, honing their skills—and physiques—to the highest possible pinnacle. Their sequestered settlements give them the privacy to pursue their ascetic lifestyles, though peches are surprisingly unperturbed by well-meaning visitors. Peches might even honor an especially skilled guest with a gift: one of their highly coveted stone crafts, created through years, if not decades, of labor. For outsiders who cause trouble, however, peches offer only the full force of their supernatural strength.

Peches are short-statured humanoids with chiseled, stony physiques that become increasingly polished as they grow more skilled in their trades. Poludnica.name: Poludnica
Poludnica.publicNotes:
Don't go into the fields—so say the village elders—when the sun is highest and the sky is the blue of a robin's egg. That's when the poludnica, the noonday demon, walks the furrows, and to meet them is death.

Of course, some don't listen. At planting and at harvest, those few extra hours in the middle of the day can mean the difference between making it through the winter and starving to death. Desperation is a powerful force, and while it's just possible some old fireside legend might kill you, hunger most assuredly will. When need isn't at play, greed does a good impression, and pride too. Just a little more work, a little bigger harvest, that little bit extra to impress—who? Yourself? Your spouse? Parents, neighbors, or even your landlord?

So, some harvesters enter the fields while the sun beats down like a hammer: the desperate, the greedy, and the foolish alike, and if they're lucky, all they have to fear is heat exhaustion, sunstroke, and dehydration. If they're unlucky, they come across a lone stranger in the fields: a young woman dressed in a kaftan of purest white, so bright it hurts to look upon, with eyes blue as cornflowers. Sometimes it's a young man instead, sometimes their clothing is pale blue, sometimes they might appear as a young child or wizened elder. Always they hold a scythe, a sickle, or a pair of old pruning shears.

The poludnica asks questions—they're fond of riddles and trick questions, confusing nonsense—all while the sun glares and the fey twists in your sight like a mirage. Answer wrongly, or stay silent, and she'll clout you on the head, causing headaches or madness. Or perhaps they'll simply bring that sickle down and slice your head clean off. They'll bury the body then, right there in the fields, and the harvest that rises from that land will be the richest in a hundred years. The people will nod, and the village elders will have a new story to tell, and perhaps in a decade or two, some new fool will die in the fields. And in exchange for their presence, the harvest grows rich and ripe, and hunger stays at bay.

Poludnicas are proud and territorial fey—a deadly threat, but a manageable one on the whole, if you're wise and listen to those who know better. They guard their fields and their time closely, and view outsiders as trespassers to be dealt with. At the same time, poludnicas don't actually hate their mortal neighbors. A poludnica's relationship with "their" village has a parental bent, that of a shepherd to their sheep (including taking the occasional meal of mutton). A poludnica ensures the harvest is good and locals don't starve, which sometimes means culling the occasional fool who fails to show respect. No one's entirely sure what poludnicas get in the exchange, though. Mortals say that poludnicas dally with mortals, ensuring their line is continued onward. Given that, like all fey, poludnicas are immortal, this is likely just some farmhand's wishful thinking. Other fey simply think that poludnicas are all stuck-up and enjoy having someone in mortal terror of them. This is more plausible.

There's an old story that says that Poludnica—just a single fey in the story—was one of four sisters: the midday star. Beside her was the youngest, Zarya, the dawn star, the evening star, Vechernitsa, and the midnight star, Nochnitsa. Together, they oversaw the proper course of the hours and the transition from darkness to light and back. They rarely quarreled, though rarely saw eye to eye, either. Supposedly, a mortal caught out by a poludnica should suggest they're on an errand for one of their sisters, especially Nochnitsa, whom Poludnica never sees. The fey might suspect a ruse, but they're likelier to let the mortal go on their way than risk aggravating their sisters.

Another story claims that the noonday demons love dancing and are better at it than any mortal. When the sun is highest and the fields are empty, they dance, alone or in great gatherings. If they meet a mortal during this time, perhaps some farmer dozing the day away, they'll wake them and implore them to dance—on pain of death. A poludnica will dance from noon till dusk, but if the mortal can keep up with them through heat and exhaustion, the impressed fey will reward them richly, with blessings of good fortune, protection, and a purse of gold for good measure.

action->Riddle Lover.name: Riddle Lover
action->Riddle Lover.description:
A creature can @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.actionspf2e.Item.OX4fy22hQgUHDr0q]{Make an Impression} on a poludnica by using Nature ([[/act make-an-impression skill=nature]]), Society ([[/act make-an-impression skill=society]]), or a suitable Lore skill to pose a riddle or answer the poludnica's riddles. In addition to the usual effects of Make an Impression, a creature that succeeds at this check receives a +1 status bonus to saves against the poludnica's spells and sunstroke haze aura (+2 on a critical success). On a failure, they take a –1 status penalty instead (–2 on a critical failure).

@UUID[Compendium.pf2e.bestiary-effects.Item.OFE5ASBprpHGoaFs]{Effect: Riddle Lover}

action->Noonday Demon.name: Noonday Demon
action->Noonday Demon.description: A poludnica loses their sunstroke haze aura while in dim light or darker and is also @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.xYTAsEpcJE1Ccni3]{Slowed 1} while in complete darkness.

action->Sunstroke Haze.name: Sunstroke Haze
action->Sunstroke Haze.description:
10 feet. A poludnica is surrounded by a shimmering haze of light and heat. Any creature that enters or begins its turn in the emanation must attempt a @Check[fortitude|dc:26] save. Regardless of the result, the creature doesn't need to make further saves against sunstroke haze for 1 minute. During the hour when the sun is at its zenith, even if the poludnica can't see it, the emanation increases to 30 feet.

Critical Success The creature is unaffected.

Success The creature is @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.MIRkyAjyBeXivMa7]{Enfeebled 1} for 1 round.

Failure The creature becomes @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.HL2l2VRSaQHu9lUw]{Fatigued} and is enfeebled 1 for as long as it's fatigued.

Critical Failure As failure, but @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.MIRkyAjyBeXivMa7]{Enfeebled 2}.

action->Cornfield Passage.name: Cornfield Passage
action->Cornfield Passage.description: The poludnica ignores difficult terrain due to vegetation.

action->Harvest Dance.name: Harvest Dance
action->Harvest Dance.description: The poludnica raises their scythe in a whirling dance. The poludnica Strides twice. At any point during the movement, they make a scythe Strike against up to two different targets; if either of these attacks is a critical hit, that target is also @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.4D2KBtexWXa6oUMR]{Drained 1}.

Puka.name: Puka
Puka.publicNotes:
A puka's true form is unknown to all, save perhaps the Eldest. These private and tricksy shapeshifters almost always wear another shape, and they're invisible when not transformed. Pukas most commonly appear as fine black horses with golden eyes, often in full tack, approaching unsuspecting mortals and enticing them to take a ride. When a puka succeeds in coaxing a rider onto their back, they launch into a gallop far faster than any horse could sprint, taking their unfortunate rider on a wild and terrifying—but ultimately harmless—journey before dropping them off exactly where they were picked up. They play similar pranks in their other forms: leading hunters on a merry chase through darkened woods as a fox or wolf, tempting late-night tavern goers as a beautiful humanoid, or taunting mortal animals as an uncatchable hare.

Any animal form a puka takes is covered in slick black fur. Even in their humanoid guises, their hair remains similarly shiny and dark, and they always include some tell-tale animalistic features, such as a horse's ears or a fox's tail.

action->Unknowable Truth.name: Unknowable Truth
action->Unknowable Truth.description: Except when transformed with Change Shape, a puka is invisible and intangible, able to move through the Universe but unable to interact with physical objects or creatures except to speak. Even then, a creature must succeed at a @Check[perception|dc:20] check to hear an invisible puka's voice.

action->Change Shape.name: Change Shape
action->Change Shape.description:
The puka takes on the appearance of one of the following creatures: a Tiny fox, hare, house cat, or raven; a Small dog, goat, or humanoid (most often a gnome or goblin); a Medium wolf or humanoid (most often an elf or human); or a Large horse. The humanoid shapes always include minor animalistic features. The puka keeps their normal Strikes, though their hoof strike deals slashing damage instead of bludgeoning in shapes with claws.

@Localize[PF2E.NPC.Abilities.Glossary.ChangeShape]

action->Wild Bolt.name: Wild Bolt
action->Wild Bolt.description: The puka Strides five times. They can't use Wild Bolt again for [[/gmr 1d4 #Recharge Wild Bolt]]{1d4 rounds}.

action->Wild Ride.name: Wild Ride
action->Wild Ride.description:
Frequency once per day

Requirements The puka is invisible or in the shape of a horse, and is not in an encounter

Effect The puka bursts into a run. Their land Speed becomes 90 feet until an hour passes, they stop moving, they enter an encounter, or they take damage, whichever comes first. Moving at this Speed nonstop for the full hour, the puka can typically cover 20–30 miles. If the puka bears a rider, that rider can't move from their mounted position or be harmed in any way until the Wild Ride ends. An unwilling rider can attempt to get off as soon as the puka starts moving, but must succeed at a @Check[acrobatics|dc:20] check or Reflex save.

Puntzelken.name: Puntzelken
Puntzelken.publicNotes:
A puntzelken is a short, stocky creature, roughly the size of an adult dwarf, and resembles nothing so much as an anthropomorphic egg. Puntzelkens are usually encountered near mortal settlements, where they seek out vantage points that offer opportunities to converse with passersby: bridges, fence posts, or walls alongside well-traveled roads. Despite their enthusiasm for social interaction, most puntzelkens come across as condescending and arrogant, seemingly engaging in conversation for the sole purpose of lording their knowledge over others.

Slow and uncoordinated, puntzelkens generally avoid combat, using their innate magic to flee if a confrontation turns violent. A provoked puntzelken, however, can prove a capable combatant, viciously pummeling enemies with the silver spoon-like implement they carry as a walking stick.

weapon->+1 Silver Spoon.name: +1 Silver Spoon
weapon->+1 Silver Spoon.description: This long piece of wood can aid in walking and deliver a mighty blow.

action->Falling Vulnerability.name: Falling Vulnerability
action->Falling Vulnerability.description: A puntzelken doubles any damage it takes from falling, before applying its weakness to bludgeoning damage.

action->Unstable.name: Unstable
action->Unstable.description: A puntzelken takes a –2 circumstance penalty to their DCs against attempts to [[/act reposition]], [[/act shove]], or [[/act trip]] them and to their saves against forced movement.

action->Confident Ramble.name: Confident Ramble
action->Confident Ramble.description:
A puntzelken's unwavering certainty is so strong that they sway the minds of others. The puntzelken spends 1 minute expounding on a topic related to one of their Lore skills, making obviously wrong claims. Any creature that pays attention or engages them in conversation must attempt a @Check[will|dc:22] save. Regardless of the outcome, the creature is temporarily immune to Confident Rambles for 1 hour.

Critical Success The creature is unconvinced and gains a +1 circumstance bonus to its saves and DCs against the puntzelken's Deception, Diplomacy, and Intimidation skill actions for 1 hour.

Success The creature is unconvinced.

Failure The creature believes the puntzelken's claims for 1 minute. It can attempt a new saving throw if presented with clear evidence against the puntzelken's claims but can't attempt more than one save per piece of evidence. Failed saving throws don't extend the effect's duration.

Critical Failure As failure, but the duration is 1 hour.

action->Curse of Fragility.name: Curse of Fragility
action->Curse of Fragility.description:
Frequency once per day

Effect The puntzelken attempts to curse a creature within 60 feet. The target attempts a @Check[will|dc:22] save.

Critical Success The creature is unaffected.

Success The creature gains the puntzelken's weakness to bludgeoning damage and falling vulnerability for 1 round.

Failure As success, but the effect lasts for 24 hours.

Critical Failure As success, but the effect lasts for 1 week.

Queen Sluagh.name: Queen Sluagh
Queen Sluagh.publicNotes:
A queen sluagh grows more powerful by devouring souls collected from underlings or drained directly through her proboscis. The muscular tongue inside is tipped with a cartilaginous, barbed quill that feeds the queen not only the soul, but the strengths of its owner.

A soul about to leave its physical body gives off a peculiar scent, usually unnoticed by mortal creatures. But the undead fey called sluagh can smell and track down its location with frightening ease. Unlike most fey, sluagh are undead, possessing strong connections to void energy and mortal souls. Sluagh collect the souls of those close to death and bring them to feed their queen.

Most sluagh appear bald-headed, with rounded ears, sharp teeth, glossy black eyes, and scrawny bodies. Their rib cages show through their skin, which is translucent and soft as velvet.

Sluagh can become ghostly and incorporeal for brief periods. They use this power to stalk their prey to great effect. Sometimes the glimpse of a sluagh is mistaken for a ghost sighting.

action->Soulscent (Imprecise) 200 feet.name: Soulscent (Imprecise) 200 feet
action->Soulscent (Imprecise) 200 feet.description: The sluagh is aware of all doomed creatures, dying creatures, and creatures that died within the last hour within the listed range.

action->Voice of the Soul.name: Voice of the Soul
action->Voice of the Soul.description: A sluagh queen knows any language of a creature whose soul they've devoured and can perfectly mimic its voice by attempting a Deception check to [[/act lie options=voice-of-the-soul]], with a +4 circumstance bonus.

action->Call of the Damned.name: Call of the Damned
action->Call of the Damned.description: The queen sends out shriek to all sluagh within 1 mile, summoning them to her. This typically calls [[/gmr 2d4 #Sluagh Reapers]] @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.feybound-bestiary.Actor.uURI8Netd0ytD9vc]{Sluagh Reapers}. If the queen is facing foes strong enough to threaten her, these are likely too weak to pose a threat but can assist by fetching items or getting in enemies' way.

action->Eat Soul.name: Eat Soul
action->Eat Soul.description: The queen touches a dying creature or a creature that died within the past 1 hour with her proboscis. If the target is dying, it must attempt a @Check[fortitude|dc:41] save; on a failure, its dying value increases by 2 (3 on a critical failure). If the target is dead, the queen automatically devours its soul. Unless the queen is destroyed, the target can't be returned to life through any means, even powerful magic such as a @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.spells-srd.Item.6dDtGIUerazSHIOu]{Wish} ritual.

action->Ghostly Swoop.name: Ghostly Swoop
action->Ghostly Swoop.description: The queen sluagh becomes incorporeal until the start of their next turn, and Flies up to their fly Speed. While incorporeal, they are immune to precision damage, and have resistance 10 to all damage (except force, @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.equipment-srd.Item.JQdwHECogcTzdd8R]{Ghost Touch}, or vitality); this resistance is doubled against non-magical damage.The sluagh queen can't use Ghostly Swoop again for [[/gmr 1d4 #Recharge Ghostly Swoop]]{1d4 rounds}.

action->Soul Theft.name: Soul Theft
action->Soul Theft.description:
Requirements The queen has a creature @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.kWc1fhmv9LBiTuei]{Grabbed} or @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.VcDeM8A5oI6VqhbM]{Restrained} with her proboscis

Effect The queen devours a portion of the required creature's soul and steals some of its ability. The target attempts a @Check[fortitude|dc:41] save. The queen gains temporary HP equal to the total amount of HP the target loses from the result of its save, including any HP lost from being drained.

Critical Success The creature is unaffected.

Success The creature takes half damage and is @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.4D2KBtexWXa6oUMR]{Drained 1}.

Failure The creature takes @Damage[5d8[void]] damage and is drained 1 and @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.3uh1r86TzbQvosxv]{Doomed 1}. The queen steals a spell slot or training. If she steals a spell from a prepared caster, she transfers the spell to herself; if she steals from a spontaneous caster, she gains a prepared spell of the appropriate level and expends one of the creature's spell slots of that level. If she steals training, she chooses from the target's Perception, attack modifier, or any skill. For 24 hours, she gains a +2 status bonus to that statistic, and the target takes a –2 status penalty to it. The queen can have any number of stolen abilities, but only one from each creature.

Critical Failure As failure, but double damage.

Remacera.name: Remacera
Remacera.publicNotes:
Remaceras are mysterious fey who represent the natural cycle of transformative rebirth and metamorphosis. They believe that the cycle of reincarnation is the greatest expression of rebirth and revel in opportunities to send other creatures down this path. To a remacera, acts of violence are akin to scavengers and bacteria helping dead organisms decompose—and there may be some truth to this, as it isn't uncommon to find strange blossoms and fruits in their wake.

Remaceras take the form of enormous caterpillars with striking patterns and serene human faces. Their calm visages are shattered when they stretch their jaws unnaturally wide to reveal a mouthful of deadly, sharklike teeth, which vibrate at high frequencies to damage and disorient foes. The most ancient remaceras can grow as long as 13 feet and weigh thousands of pounds.

Despite their violent proclivities, remaceras savor the opportunity to have profound conversations with intelligent creatures. They seldom hold those who slay them in contempt, for they too receive renewal in death. Those who undergo a crisis of belief and turn nihilistic return as escorites.

action->Destined Renewal.name: Destined Renewal
action->Destined Renewal.description: A remacera is permanently affected by their own curse of renewal. When a remacera dies, after 1 minute, their new body appears [[/gmr 1d20 #miles]] miles from where they died. They can also choose to retain their current form.

action->Curse of Renewal.name: Curse of Renewal
action->Curse of Renewal.description: A creature damaged by a remacera's jaws must succeed at a @Check[will|dc:24] save or be afflicted with the curse of renewal. A creature that dies while affected by this curse is subjected to the effects of a successful @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.spells-srd.Item.gIVaSCrLhhBzGHQY]{Reincarnate} ritual that takes effect after 1 minute, regardless of whether the soul is willing to return.

action->Murderous Rhapsody.name: Murderous Rhapsody
action->Murderous Rhapsody.description:
When a creature the remacera reduced to 0 Hit Points dies, the remacera gains 10 temporary Hit Points that last for 1 minute and is @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.nlCjDvLMf2EkV2dl]{Quickened} for as long as they have these temporary Hit Points. They can use the extra action only to Stride or Strike.

@UUID[Compendium.pf2e.bestiary-effects.Item.nPpoBcXXcT1SA4L9]{Effect: Murderous Rhapsody}

action->New Growth.name: New Growth
action->New Growth.description:
The remacera spawns tiny, larval remaceras within a creature they can see within 100 feet. That creature must attempt a @Check[fortitude|dc:24|options:inflicts:clumsy,inflicts:sickened,inflicts:off-guard] save.

Critical Success The creature is unaffected.

Success The creature becomes @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.i3OJZU2nk64Df3xm]{Clumsy 1} for 1 round as some larvae spawn on its skin before harmlessly falling off.

Failure As success, and the creature is @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.fesd1n5eVhpCSS18]{Sickened 2} as several larvae burrow out of its skin.

Critical Failure As failure, but the creature is @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.fesd1n5eVhpCSS18]{Sickened 3} and @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.AJh5ex99aV6VTggg]{Off-Guard} while it remains sickened.

action->Ultrasonic Ululation.name: Ultrasonic Ululation
action->Ultrasonic Ululation.description:
Frequency once per round

Requirements The remacera has a creature @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.kWc1fhmv9LBiTuei]{Grabbed} or @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.VcDeM8A5oI6VqhbM]{Restrained} in their jaws

Effect The creature takes @Damage[(2d10+8)[sonic]] damage with a @Check[fortitude|dc:24|basic|options:inflicts:stupefied] save. A creature that fails is also @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.e1XGnhKNSQIm5IXg]{Stupefied 1} for 1 round (1 minute on a critical failure).

Risen Fetch.name: Risen Fetch
Risen Fetch.publicNotes:
Echoes of a corrupted undead soul can be used to spawn a fetch as well. A risen fetch appears more as their source did in life than as an undead.

A fetch is a twisted, deviant simulacrum of a humanoid creature that exists or existed at one point on the Universe. While there are rumors of fetches who are reflections of beings from other planes, if such exist, they must still be duplicates of a sapient creature. A fetch can manifest spontaneously when a powerful person undergoes a significant emotional event or dies, either while in the First World or in an area significantly influenced by that plane. However, they've also been created by potent entities like the Eldest to torment and vex those who've annoyed them. While a fetch manifests from a soul's "reflection," and as such bears a striking resemblance to that soul's appearance, they have no true memories of their own. They hold fragments of false remembrances from their source, as if they experienced them in a half-remembered dream—which ensures the fetch is enraged by and jealous of their original.

A fetch is similar in appearance to the creature whose soul spawned them, except that they often possess fey-like features such as pointed ears, plant elements, or supernatural grace. A fetch who seeks to impersonate a still-living source must take care to hide these features and manifest a fetch weapon that their living template wields.

When a fetch dies, they fade away along with all of their manifested items into a bloom of plant life, their soul instantly recycled into the First World, leaving behind a patch of weeds and thorny flowers roughly in the shape they held while alive.

Sangoi.name: Sangoi
Sangoi.publicNotes: With their nocturnal habits, taste for blood, and proclivity for haunting towns and graveyards in the dead of night, it's unsurprising that sangois are often mistaken for vampires. These smaller fey hunt by following the sounds of their victims' hearts, preferring humanoid victims but settling for animal blood if necessary. They wear roughly cut animal hides to stay warm and are often mistaken for prowling coyotes or wildcats when glimpsed from a window on a cold, misty night.

action->Sunlight Transparency.description: Sunlight causes the sangoi to partially fade from view, growing feeble and translucent. While exposed to direct sunlight, the sangoi is @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.DmAIPqOBomZ7H95W]{Concealed}, @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.i3OJZU2nk64Df3xm]{Clumsy 1}, and @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.MIRkyAjyBeXivMa7]{Enfeebled 1}.

action->Blood Rage.description:

action->Bloodsense.name: Bloodsense
action->Bloodsense.description: The sangoi can hear the beating hearts and smell the rushing blood of all living creatures as an imprecise sense within the listed range. They can detect creatures taking persistent bleed damage as a precise sense.

action->Curse of Misery.name: Curse of Misery
action->Curse of Misery.description: A creature hit by a sangoi's claws Strike must succeed at a @Check[will|dc:22] save or become cursed for 1 minute. This curse imparts a –1 status penalty to a victim's AC and saving throws against the sangoi who cursed them. In addition, when a cursed victim attempts the flat check to recover from any persistent bleed damage, they must roll twice and take the worse result; this is a misfortune effect.

action->Sneak Attack.name: Sneak Attack
action->Sneak Attack.description: The sangoi deals an additional 2d6 precision damage to @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.AJh5ex99aV6VTggg]{Off-Guard} creatures.

action->Vicious Draught.name: Vicious Draught
action->Vicious Draught.description:

Effect The sangoi latches onto the creature's open wound, drinking their blood. They attempt a jaws Strike against the target; if the target is willing, the Strike automatically hits. If the Strike hits, the persistent bleed condition ends, the target is @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.4D2KBtexWXa6oUMR]{Drained 1}, and the sangoi regains Hit Points equal to the target's level, gaining any excess HP as temporary HP. Taking a Vicious Draught from a creature that's already drained doesn't restore any HP to the sangoi but increases the victim's drained value by 1 (to a maximum of @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.4D2KBtexWXa6oUMR]{Drained 4}).

If the sangoi is in a Blood Rage and the jaws Strike reduces the target to 0 HP, the victim must attempt a @Check[fortitude|dc:22] save. On a failure, the sangoi tears out the target's heart and devours it, killing it instantly. This is a death effect.

Sard.name: Sard
Sard.publicNotes: An immense, gnarled tree awoken with raw, primal power by one of the Eldest of the First World, this legendary Tane skitters on huge, spidery roots and thrashes their branches. Fiery lightning courses within their blackened bark, a living manifestation of the violent clash between ancient forest and stormy sky. Sards are created as living siege engines, awoken by the Eldest when the target of their ire tries to hide behind stone walls and high battlements. The blood-red lightning that runs through a sard's twisted trunk instead of sap makes short work of such mortal defenses, great arcs of electricity tearing through stone and those that hide behind it. As representations of the cataclysmic destruction of serene beauty, sards take cruel glee in their work.

action->Splintering Death.description: When the sard dies, its body explodes in a @Template[emanation|distance:30]. All creatures in the area take @Damage[10d6[electricity],10d6[piercing]|options:area-damage]{10d6 electricity damage and 10d6 piercing damage} (@Check[reflex|dc:43|basic|options:area-effect] save). action->Lightning-Struck Curse.name: Lightning-Struck Curse
action->Lightning-Struck Curse.description:

Old and well-traveled, a seilenos has seen many things in their existence. They remember when the First World was the only world. They've seen empires come and go, godlings rise and fall. With the legs, ears, and tail of a horse, gnarled beard, and skin as weathered as old oak, many mortals mistake depictions of seilenoi for arboreals or green men.

A seilenos might act as mercurial judge, fun-loving master of ceremonies, or ruthless bandit leader. Never-before-seen spectacles of beauty, music, and art compel a seilenos's attention, and they have ways of inspiring those they meet to follow their creative pursuits to the extreme. Most seilenoi view the idea of combat as amusing, but should they become roused to anger, their power is terrifying.

Selkie.name: Selkie
Selkie.publicNotes:
The haunting songs that sometimes accompany pods of seals are from selkies, fey who freely shift between human and seal forms. Their natural forms belong fully to neither world, sporting a mix of human and seal features.

Selkies move through the water and on the shore with equal ease, and seaside communities often talk of them as though they were the tide itself. Despite these poetic associations, however, the life of a selkie exists far beyond the imagination of land-bound mortals. For selkies, losing either the land or the sea is to lose a part of themselves. They eagerly seek kinship with others who exist in multiple worlds and are often found as surprise guests at the celebrations of azarketis or merfolk.

weapon->Sealbone Dagger.name: Sealbone Dagger
weapon->Sealbone Dagger.description: This small, bladed weapon is held in one hand and used to stab a creature in close combat. It can also be thrown.

armor->Sealskin Coat.name: Sealskin Coat
armor->Sealskin Coat.description: A mix of furs, sturdy hide, and sometimes molded boiled leather, this armor provides protection due to its layers of leather, though its bulkiness slows the wearer down and decreases mobility.

action->Sealskin Coat.name: Sealskin Coat
action->Sealskin Coat.description:
A selkie can slip their seal pelt on and off as a sealskin coat. They're permanently bound to it and can sense its location if separated (as the locate spell). While wearing their sealskin coat, the selkie is immune to mild, severe, and extreme cold, and treats incredible cold as severe cold. They can also speak with seals (as speak with animals). When the selkie uses Change Shape, they must draw their sealskin coat around themself to become a seal or fully remove it to become a human. They can't leave their human form if their sealskin coat isn't in their possession.

If their sealskin coat is destroyed, the selkie feels its loss as an ever-present wound. They take a −1 status penalty to all attacks and saving throws, but they gain a +1 status bonus to seaborn yearning's DC and their edge of mourning deals @Damage[2d6[mental]] damage instead of 1d6.

Melee 1 fist +14 (agile, finesse, nonlethal, unarmed)

Damage 1d4+6 bludgeoning

action->Deep Breath.name: Deep Breath

action->Edge of Mourning.name: Edge of Mourning
action->Edge of Mourning.description: A selkie's sealbone dagger Strikes deal an additional 1d6 mental damage.

action->Seaborn Yearning.name: Seaborn Yearning
action->Seaborn Yearning.description: 30 feet. When a selkie is outside of their home waters, their yearning for home radiates from them. A creature that enters or starts its turn in the aura must succeed at a @Check[will|dc:22|options:area-effect] save or become unable to benefit from emotion effects for 1 minute (though they can still take penalties or damage from emotion effects); on a critical failure, the duration is 24 hours. Regardless of the result, the creature is temporarily immune to seaborn yearning for 24 hours.

Shadow Collector.name: Shadow Collector
Shadow Collector.publicNotes:
When the traitor Count Ranalc was banished to the Netherworld, loyal sprites, gnomes, and nymphs of his court were exiled alongside him. Millennia in the shadows changed these courtiers into shadow collectors—mirrials in their own tongue. These small fey prowl the Netherworld and its borderlands, searching out wayward shadows to add to their vast collections.

According to legend, when the fey who would become mirrials first arrived in the Netherworld, their new shadowy home's lack of light meant they no longer cast the same twisting shadows they'd had in the First World. Despairing, the fey crept into the Universe, stalking midnight forests and dreary foothills to steal the shadows of unsuspecting mortals. When these first few stolen shadows cast barely a single foot of darkness, they took more and more, weaving their treasures together until they had terrifying shadows the size of dragons and giants.

Failure The collector steals a scrap of the shadow, increasing the size of their shadow menagerie aura by 5 feet for 1 minute.

Critical Failure As failure, but the aura is increased by 10 feet and the collector steals the target's shadow permanently. The shadow is returned if the shadow collector dies or takes a Dismiss action to release the shadow.

action->Slip Behind.name: Slip Behind
action->Slip Behind.description: The shadow collector slips into a creature's shadow, teleporting to a space adjacent to that creature within 15 feet. The target or its items can't be emitting magical light, and if the target is within an area of magical light the shadow collector must choose a destination that puts the target between them and the light's source.

action->Sneak Attack.name: Sneak Attack

A creature who critically fails is also @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.conditionitems.Item.XgEqL1kFApUbl5Z2]{Blinded} for 1 round. The shadow collector's aura decreases by 10 feet.

Sluagh Reaper.name: Sluagh Reaper
Sluagh Reaper.publicNotes:
Most sluagh are reapers: powerful killers subservient to their queen. After they collect souls on a hunt, they dutifully return their plunder to the queen. Though quite clever, they're inscrutable, lacking the whimsy and sociability that characterize many living fey. They do show merriment on occasion though, giggling as their claws draw closer to their quarry's throat.

A soul about to leave its physical body gives off a peculiar scent, usually unnoticed by mortal creatures. But the undead fey called sluagh can smell and track down its location with frightening ease. Unlike most fey, sluagh are undead, possessing strong connections to void energy and mortal souls. Sluagh collect the souls of those close to death and bring them to feed their queen.

Most sluagh appear bald-headed, with rounded ears, sharp teeth, glossy black eyes, and scrawny bodies. Their rib cages show through their skin, which is translucent and soft as velvet.

Sluagh can become ghostly and incorporeal for brief periods. They use this power to stalk their prey to great effect. Sometimes the glimpse of a sluagh is mistaken for a ghost sighting.

action->Ghostly Swoop.name: Ghostly Swoop
action->Ghostly Swoop.description: The sluagh reaper becomes incorporeal until the start of their next turn and Flies up to their fly Speed. While incorporeal, they are immune to precision damage and have resistance 10 to all damage (except force, @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.equipment-srd.Item.JQdwHECogcTzdd8R]{Ghost Touch}, or vitality); this resistance is doubled against non-magical damage. The sluagh reaper can't use Ghostly Swoop again for [[/gmr 1d4 #Recharge Ghostly Swoop]]{1d4 rounds}.

The sluagh reaper touches a dying creature or a creature that died within the past hour. If the target is a dying creature, it must attempt a @Check[fortitude|dc:28] save; on a failure, its dying value increases by 1 (2 on a critical failure). If the target is dead, the sluagh automatically imprisons its soul in a small, grimy sack that keeps stolen souls fresh.

The sack is magically locked. Any sluagh can open it without difficulty, but any others must [[/act pick-a-lock dc=35]]{Pick the Lock} or use @UUID[Compendium.pf2e.spells-srd.Item.9HpwDN4MYQJnW0LG]{Dispel Magic} (5th level; counteract DC 32). A creature can Interact to empty an unlocked sack, which frees the souls but doesn't return them to life. While a soul is imprisoned, it can't be brought back to life by any means short of a wish ritual or similar magic. The sack can hold 12 souls at a time. Sluagh reapers typically attempt to deliver the souls to a queen sluagh so she can devour them.

Sorrow Stitcher.name: Sorrow Stitcher
Sorrow Stitcher.publicNotes:
Sorrow stitchers, as their name suggests, are beings of intense sadness. Ages ago, their forebears transgressed against one of the great powers of the First World, and as a result, their entire people were exiled to the Universe, barred from returning in perpetuity. So severe is the denial of the joy and mirth of the First World that sorrow stitchers have lost the ability to experience any feeling beyond fear and sorrow.

Most sorrow stitchers spend their time seeking out things that might bring happiness, even though nothing can ever restore that emotion to them. They're especially drawn to areas of concentrated joy—parks, fairgrounds, parades and the like. Their proximity to mortal population centers can be troublesome, as their frustration over being unable to experience happiness often leads them to lash out at the very displays of joy that entice them.

Sorrow stitchers are pale, sallow folk. They shroud themselves in colorful patchwork cloaks, fruitlessly hoping the garish colors will bring them some measure of joy. Each sorrow stitcher also carries a magical needle that can briefly capture threads of fate. They use these needles to sew a mortal's happiness onto their own heart, hoping to steal it for themselves. Lacking the true power to weave fate, however, these threads quickly fray, leaving the sorrow stitcher more forlorn than ever.

Sporgout.languages: Can't speak, Speak with plants, Telepathy 100 feet (infected creatures only)
Sporgout.publicNotes:
Countless myths warn about the dangers of stepping into a ring of mushrooms, but few extend this caution to the hidden threat that often lurks beneath them. Sporgouts are born when mushroom colonies aiding in the decay of a corpse consume vast amounts of primal energy, whether because the body was a being of primal magic (like a leshy or arboreal) or because it died in an area of strong fey influence. These colonies become so infused with magic that they attain their own sentience as a singular sporgout, lying in wait underground to ambush those who carelessly draw near. Though once believed to be undead, sporgouts are not reanimated corpses; while they absorb the nutrients and magic of their host body, they are wholly new creatures.

Sporgouts resemble unnatural humanoids with bodies like rotting logs or burned or petrified wood, covered in a colorful riot of strange fungi and lichens. They have no eyes or mouths, though they turn their heads as if mimicking beings who use such features to communicate. They have little interest in interacting with strangers and are often mistaken for solitary creatures, but like mundane mushrooms, sporgouts can and do communicate with each other across long distances through a mycorrhizal network.

Spriggan Bully.publicNotes:
The typical spriggan is a bully who prefers to take live prisoners in fights, but only to ensure that they have a large stock of living victims to torment, tease, and abuse. They train to use their weapons in nonlethal, but still painful, ways.

When gnomes left the First World, many embraced and adapted to life in the Universe, but not all were so resilient. Those who instead hardened their hearts in this time formed insular communities that prioritized survival by any means necessary. Over generations, these communities lost their interest in joy and beauty, diverging into sour creatures called spriggans. In exchange for this loss, they gained an immunity to the Bleaching and the ability to grow in size for short periods of time to increase their odds of survival—or better menace their victims. Over time, spriggans' culture of ruthless pragmatism has become one of sadistic cruelty, their only joy derived from visiting harm upon others.

When gnomes left the First World, many embraced and adapted to life in the Universe, but not all were so resilient. Those who instead hardened their hearts in this time formed insular communities that prioritized survival by any means necessary. Over generations, these communities lost their interest in joy and beauty, diverging into sour creatures called spriggans. In exchange for this loss, they gained an immunity to the Bleaching and the ability to grow in size for short periods of time to increase their odds of survival—or better menace their victims. The greatest secret of the murderous trickster known as Spring-Heeled Jack is that he isn't a unique creature. Instead, he's one of a rare type of fey native to the First World who enjoy causing bloody mayhem in the Universe. These fey are so rare (and so distrustful of each other's company) that two have never been seen together; the mistaken assumption that only a single spring-heeled jack exists is therefore entirely understandable. The fact that sightings occur across Ustalav (and beyond), across centuries of time, is ascribed to the trickster's long lifespan and mysterious ability to travel quickly, or to the belief that there's no such creature, merely an urban legend that twisted minds attempt to bring to life through costumes, magic, and a series of murders and mayhem. Even in fear-drenched Ustalav, no one has yet guessed that multiple spring-heeled jacks exist.

Spring-heeled jacks are cruel-eyed, hairy fey with vaguely humanoid shapes and extra features that cause them to be easily mistaken for demons or devils. Glowing eyes, cloven hooves, menacing horns, and a pointed tail combine to create the mien of a wicked imp; their love of sudden and sadistic violence completes the impression. Almost all have jet-black skin and fur, though a few exceptions might exist.

In the nighttime conditions they enjoy, spring-heeled jacks typically hide their features in tattered cloaks, appearing as a hunched elder or a youth. Such a disguise rarely holds up to any scrutiny, but that doesn't matter much to the spring-heeled jack, who only needs something that offers just enough doubt for their target to move within striking distance—which can be much greater than most creatures realize. Once close enough, the spring-heeled jack leaps startling distances in the flicker of an eye to easily slash at a victim who had, until that moment, considered themself safe.

While most nymphs bond with a natural feature, such as a tree, pool, or cave, horai are rare nymphs associated with a specific time—solstices and equinoxes—rather than a location. Horai erect simple astronomical calendars near their homes, which they use to mark the moment when the sun reaches its highest or lowest point in the sky. A hora tied to the summer solstice grows more powerful as the sun reaches its height, while becoming sickly and weak during the winter solstice. The opposite holds true for winter horai, who are weak in summer and strong in winter. Meanwhile, autumn and spring horai draw power near the autumnal and vernal equinoxes, respectively, becoming weaker around the opposite equinox.

Summer horai appear constantly bathed in sunlight, with skin and clothing of red, orange, and yellow, like the sunlight of high summer.

Winter, Spring and Autumn Horai

The statistics here are for summer horai, but you can represent the other three types of horai with minor alterations.

Winter horai have resistance to cold rather than fire, and their strikes deal cold damage instead of fire; are winter bound (impeded during summer months); and have Winter's Rescue (+4 during the month of the winter solstice, +2 on the months just before and after, +1 in spring and autumn, and no benefit during the summer). For a winter hora queen, being tied to the land improves the environment in winter and twists it in summer.

Autumn horai have resistance to void instead of fire, and their strikes deal void damage instead of fire; are autumn bound (impeded during spring); and have Autumn's Rescue (+4 during the month of the autumnal equinox, +2 on the months just before and after, +1 in summer and winter, and no benefit during spring). For an autumn hora queen, tied to the land improves the environment in autumn and twists it in spring.

Spring horai have no resistance, and their strikes deal vitality damage instead of fire (harming only creatures with void healing, as normal); are spring bound (impeded during autumn); and have Spring's Rescue (+4 during the month of the vernal equinox, +2 on the months just before and after, +1 in winter and summer, and no benefit during autumn). For a spring hora queen, tied to the land improves the environment in spring and twists it in autumn.

In the First World's first few centuries, even before the full creation of the Universe, svartalfars lived among the other fey. No records exist of their exact appearance at that time, though many scholars believe they had typical elven features. At some point in the distant past, the majority of these svartalfars participated in some unknown heinous acts, and their entire people were summarily exiled to the Netherworld. That shadowy plane soon warped svartalfars in both body and mind, turning their skin pale gray and hairless and their thoughts cruel and practical. Present-day svartalfars are born with some innate shadow magic.

Svartalfar communities in the Netherworld are small, featuring tall, slender buildings and subterranean chambers. The largest structures are operated by powerful guilds of assassins and bounty hunters that the community takes great pride in. Guild members are deadly serious about any contracts they agree upon, working with brutal efficiency to find (and often dispose of) their targets. When a svartalfar fails to complete their mission, they are usually publicly executed by their kin.

Svartalfar who hone their connection to the Netherworld might train as shadowskeins, manipulators of shadow and darkness. Shadowskeins tap into the occult power of shadows to create umbral illusions.

In the First World's first few centuries, even before the full creation of the Universe, svartalfars lived among the other fey. No records exist of their exact appearance at that time, though many scholars believe they had typical elven features. At some point in the distant past, the majority of these svartalfars participated in some unknown heinous acts, and their entire people were summarily exiled to the Netherworld. That shadowy plane soon warped svartalfars in both body and mind, turning their skin pale gray and hairless and their thoughts cruel and practical. Present-day svartalfars are born with some innate shadow magic.

Svartalfar communities in the Netherworld are small, featuring tall, slender buildings and subterranean chambers. The largest structures are operated by powerful guilds of assassins and bounty hunters that the community takes great pride in. Guild members are deadly serious about any contracts they agree upon, working with brutal efficiency to find (and often dispose of) their targets. When a svartalfar fails to complete their mission, they are usually publicly executed by their kin.

Thrasfyr.publicNotes:
As ferocious in temperament as they are bizarre in appearance, thrasfyrs resemble six-limbed bears with bull-like horns, draconic scales, and a fire-breathing serpent for a tail. Every thrasfyr is wrapped in animated chains, reflections of its fundamental nature as a bound creature that it uses to likewise bind its foes. Like all the Tane, thrasfyrs were created as living weapons by the Eldest. With the ancient wars they were born to fight long ended, most thrasfyrs slumber in rugged, uninhabited regions.

Though they are engineered beings, thrasfyrs are still living beasts that need to eat, drink, and sleep; they do age, as well, though they live such long lives that a thrasfyr succumbing to old age is vanishingly rare.

Ujdavipr.publicNotes:
Ujdaviprs serve as spies and messengers for powerful fey creatures, be they nymph queens, norns, or even one of the Eldest. They travel throughout the First World and to planes beyond, collecting important information or spying on dangerous creatures for their masters. During feuds and squabbles between powerful fey, ujdaviprs also scout and deliver messages on their leader's behalf.

An ujdavipr's true form is a humanoid with slit pupils, fangs resembling those of a snake, and reptilian scales of any color. Ujdaviprs are capable of shape-shifting into a snake, a scaled flying squirrel, or a hybrid form with qualities of both, as demanded by their mission. Most ujdaviprs wear hooded cloaks to keep their physical features hidden.

Closer inspection reveals glowing red eyes hidden in the morass, full of cruelty and malice. Also known as roseblood sprites, veredrams embody the thorns of the rose—danger and pain hidden amongst beauty.

Elusive, flighty, and ebullient, sprites are what many villagers first imagine when they hear the terms "fey" or "fairy."

Vexgit.name: Vexgit
Vexgit.publicNotes:
Vexgits are covered head-to-toe by a crustacean-like exoskeleton that clacks and rattles whenever they move. They delight in sabotaging the works of other creatures, often turning these works into dangerous hazards. An individual vexgit might jam a door lock, loosen the wheels on a carriage, or remove nails from a boat hull. Buildings infested by vexgits become death traps, filled with portcullises descending suddenly, water pipes exploding violently, and clock towers disgorging avalanches of gears.

Like many fey, gremlins personify a natural force of the world: entropy. It's a fundamental truth that everything breaks, that every complex system, from a machine to a society, will inevitably grind itself down to nothing. Gremlins are happy to give those complex systems a friendly shove down the stairs.

Nearly all gremlins live in the Universe, where they have fully acclimated to the plane. No one is quite certain why, but it seems likely that some long-forgotten gremlin managed to so irritate the Eldest to such a degree that their entire species was exiled—though it appears the Eldest missed a few, as some gremlins still lurk in the First World.

Gremlins are usually found in an odd, parasitic relationship with mortal communities in the Universe. They don't need to eat or sleep, don't age or sicken, and never really die—but they do need to cause trouble. It's as essential to them as food and drink are to mortals, and nowhere do they get as many chances for chaos and confusion as in a mortal settlement. Gremlins thus become pests, living on the margins of society and bedeviling anyone and anything they can get their hands on.

Wild Hunt Archer.languages: speak with animals; speak with plants
Wild Hunt Archer.publicNotes:
Wild hunt archers are androgynous humanoids have glowing green eyes, pointed ears, horns, and hair that always flows softly as if in a gentle breeze. Since they tend to be slower on foot than most of their companions, they often rely on their mounts for increased mobility. They carry no arrows, instead producing them from magical quivers that function only for them. Their bows are made of living wood.

Although some believe the wild hunt is nothing more than legend, the riders of the hunt are very real, comprised of countless lithe, horned humanoids, along with their steeds and hunting hounds. The term "wild hunt" refers to these fey as a whole, as well as to individual groups who gather at a wild hunt monarch's call to pursue their chosen quarry. The less dangerous a quarry, the more likely a monarch will impose rules to make the hunt more entertaining.

Wild Hunt Monarch.name: Wild Hunt Monarch
Wild Hunt Monarch.languages: Speak with animals, Speak with plants
Wild Hunt Monarch.publicNotes:
Each wild hunt follows a wild hunt monarch who travels between the First World and the Universe in search of new quarry. These limber and regal humanoids have elk antlers, long pointed ears, flowing hair, and luminescent green eyes. They carry long, deadly glaives, believing that ranged weapons are unnecessary—their duty is simply to deliver the killing blow after their hunters have downed the hunt's quarry with arrows and spells. Wild hunt monarchs also carry a gnarled horn which they blow to call up the hunt. Each monarch's horn produces a unique call, allowing hunters to tell each other apart when multiple hunts join together.

Although some believe the wild hunt is nothing more than legend, the riders of the hunt are very real, comprised of countless lithe, horned humanoids, along with their steeds and hunting hounds. The term "wild hunt" refers to these fey as a whole, as well as to individual groups who gather at a wild hunt monarch's call to pursue their chosen quarry. The less dangerous a quarry, the more likely a monarch will impose rules to make the hunt more entertaining.
